item.title: First $250K, Now Millions: Another Undisclosed Funding Source Surfaces in Bonito Lake Closure Fight
item.description:
Part 3: Citizen contacts with multiple state agencies point to a possible multimillion-dollar agreement with the state — with nearly $1 million reportedly already spent on design — to correct the very concerns cited in the closure proposal

Editor’s note: This is Part 3 in an ongoing Alamogordo Town News series examining City Manager Robert Stockwell’s proposal to close Bonito Lake to recreation and fence the reservoir. Part 1 examined the up-to-$1 million fence proposal, the Open Gate Agreement, and the community response. Part 2 revealed that the 2026 Legislature approved $250,000 — requested by the City itself — for shoreline and day-use improvements at the lake, an appropriation never mentioned in the closure proposal. The Commission tabled the proposal until its September 22, 2026 meeting.

A pattern is emerging in the debate over Bonito Lake’s future: resources committed to keeping the lake open keep surfacing after the fact — never in the City’s own presentation for closing it.

First it was the $250,000. As this series reported in Part 2, the 2026 Legislature approved — in full — the City’s own Commission-approved request for shoreline and day-use improvements at the lake. Senate Bill 240 was signed into law on March 11, 2026, becoming Chapter 71 of the Laws of 2026. That appropriation appeared nowhere in the August 25 agenda report recommending termination of public access and construction of up to $1 million in security fencing.

Now, information reaching this news organization suggests the $250,000 may be the smaller omission.

A possible multimillion-dollar agreement

It has recently come to the attention of this news organization that concerned citizens have contacted multiple state agencies regarding the future of Bonito Lake. Through information shared during those communications, this news organization became aware of a possible multimillion-dollar agreement between the City of Alamogordo and the New Mexico Department of Game and Fish, now the New Mexico Department of Wildlife, to address infrastructure and safety concerns at the lake.

The proposed partnership reportedly included millions of dollars in improvements — figures described to this news organization as approaching $8 million — in addition to nearly $1 million the state had already invested in design work. The proposed work may have included clearing the coffer dam and detention basin, realigning the channel, and correcting infrastructure concerns so the area could safely move toward reopening campgrounds and preserving fishing access.

The stated purpose, as described to this news organization, was straightforward: fix the infrastructure so it would be safe to move on to the campground.

If accurate, that scope of work reads as a near line-item match for the deteriorating infrastructure and uncleaned debris basins the City Manager cited as grounds for closure.

A chronology the records should confirm — or refute

Information received by this news organization describes a specific sequence of events, which multiple pending records requests to confirm.

The agreement was reportedly the product of extended negotiations between city leadership and the Department, and was said to be nearing completion at the time former acting City Manager Dr. Hernandez departed. 

Work on the agreement reportedly continued under the acting city manager who followed, and the document was ready for execution — expected to be signed in late June or July.

Information received indicates a draft agreement was in fact signed by the then-acting city manager before that official’s own departure from the City.

Rather than transmitting or honoring that executed version, City Manager Stockwell reportedly had the document sent back to be amended and reissued bearing his name to the agreement for his signature.

Whether Stockwell ever signed the reissued version — or whether the agreement was allowed to lapse, was cancelled, or remains pending with the Department — is unknown to this news organization pending confirmation via our IPRA requests. 

If this account is accurate, the implications are significant: the agreement did not sit unnoticed in a file. It was negotiated across two city administrations, an draft executed once, and returned specifically so it could carry the current City Manager’s signature — months before he presented a closure proposal that made no mention of it. An agreement a city manager asks to have reissued in his own name is not an agreement he was unaware of.

This news organization emphasizes that this chronology is drawn from information received, staff accounts and, not yet from documents yet in hand completely. The signature history — who signed, when, and what the Department did upon receipt — exists in records held by both the City and the Department, and both have now been asked to produce them.

A contractor on site

The possible agreement is not the only resource that has surfaced outside the official presentation. A contractor was recently observed working at Bonito Lake. This news organization was informed that the contractor had an active $56,000 agreement with the City, and was expected to repair the stairwell steps described as among the most serious safety concerns at the property. The current status and full scope of that agreement have not yet been confirmed but a copy of the scope of work and who is executing the work has also been requested via IPRA. 

With an active contractor agreement existing to remedy the stairwell — a hazard specifically invoked in the case for closure — that too was absent from the presentation to the Commission and is concerning. 

The state’s role and tax dollars already expended is substantial

None of this would arise in a vacuum. As reported in Part 1, the City operates under a seven-year, prepaid Open Gate Access Program agreement with the Department — the arrangement that reopened Bonito Lake to anglers in 2024 after twelve years of closure following the Little Bear Fire, and one that would reportedly obligate the City to repay the state if public access is ended early.

Information now received by this news organization further indicates that, under the Open Gate arrangement was enhanced, the Department committed to monitor and patrol the Bonito Lake area — a commitment made because the City lacked the staff to do so itself. If so, the staffing burden presented to the Commission as a reason for closure may already have an answer sitting in an existing agreement.

Counted together, that is a $250,000 appropriation, a possible agreement approaching $8 million, a contractor reportedly under active agreement for the most cited safety hazard, and a state patrol commitment — none of it disclosed to the commission nor the public in the closure presentation.

The records request

This news organization has submitted a request under the New Mexico Inspection of Public Records Act for agreements, contracts, proposed scopes of work, design documents, correspondence, cancellation records, and other documents related to Bonito Lake. A second request seeks communications and correspondence concerning these agreements among city staff, the City Manager, and city commissioners. A parallel request is being directed to the New Mexico Department of Wildlife, which holds its own copies of any draft or executed agreement, the design invoices, and the related correspondence.

What the public deserves to know

The public deserves to know what contracts or agreements existed, or remain active, to correct the safety and infrastructure concerns identified by City Manager Robert Stockwell. That accounting should include the status and intended use of the $250,000 capital outlay appropriation for shoreline access, day-use facilities, and related improvements at Bonito Lake.

If state funding, agency assistance, contractor agreements, or other resources were already available to address these concerns, the City Manager should explain why this was not part of the broader discussion before permanent closure was recommended.

If a multimillion-dollar partnership existed, or was close to being finalized, the public deserves to know what happened to it.

Before the September 22 vote, the Commission should ask, in addition to the questions raised in Part 2:

What is the current status of any infrastructure agreement with the New Mexico Department of Wildlife?

Was a version executed by the former acting city manager, and if so, why was it returned to be reissued rather than transmitted?

If the state has already invested nearly $1 million in design work, what happens to that investment — and to the City’s relationship with the Department — if the lake is fenced?

What is the status and scope of the contractor agreement for the stairwell and handrail work, and why was it not disclosed?

Did the Department’s patrol and monitoring commitments under the Open Gate Agreement factor into the claim that the City cannot oversee the area?

The City of Alamogordo, the city manager’s office, and the New Mexico Department of Wildlife did not immediately respond to requests for comment. This story will be updated as records are produced.

Join the discussion Tuesday

Residents will have a chance to discuss all of this live — and be heard before the Commission votes. The Voices of Alamogordo monthly community forum, “Keep Open Access to Bonito Lake,” will be held Tuesday, September 1, 2026 at 6:00 p.m. at Otero Arts, 1118 Indiana Avenue, Alamogordo. The forum is a community discussion on the lake’s history, purpose, and significance — and what residents can do to keep it open. Hosted by 2nd Life Media, Alamogordo Town News, and KALH Radio, the event is free and open to the public. All are welcome. Bring your questions.

item.title: City Manager Stockwell and Others to Join Community Forum on Bonito Lake Fencing Proposal Tuesday at Otero Arts
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — The future of public access to Bonito Lake takes center stage Tuesday, September 1, at 6 p.m. as Voices of Alamogordo hosts a community forum at Otero Arts, 1118 Indiana Ave. at 12th Street, to discuss a fencing proposal that would close the lake to the public.

The forum comes amid renewed controversy over the lake, which residents waited more than a decade to see reopened. Bonito Lake was closed after the 2012 Little Bear Fire, when the burn scar left no vegetation and subsequent heavy rains washed silt and gravel down the canyon into the lake . In September 2017, Alamogordo city commissioners approved an $8.6 million contract to drain, dredge, and restore the lake , and with sediment catchment basins completed to protect against future erosion, the lake was refilled in 2023 .

Even the reopening proved star-crossed. The lake was scheduled to reopen in May 2024 — with trout stocked the day before — when the Blue 2 Fire forced the area closed once again . Bonito Lake finally reopened for fishing only on August 30, 2024 .

Barely two years later, the lake’s future is again in question. City Manager Stockwell has proposed building a fence around the reservoir, citing unsafe conditions, worsening infrastructure, and a lack of funds to maintain the area . Stockwell has argued the city’s primary focus should be preserving the lake as a dependable water supply, and that restricting access would help ensure it remains a reliable source .

The proposal has already drawn pushback. When Stockwell presented the closure at a recent commission meeting, some commissioners questioned whether fencing off the lake is the best way to address the problem, with one suggesting that if the campground is unusable, the city should close the campground rather than the lake, noting the area is a tourist attraction. The City Commission tabled a vote on the proposal until its September 22 meeting — making Tuesday’s forum a timely opportunity for public input before commissioners take up the matter.

City Manager Robert Stockwell will join the panel to explain his proposal and the reasoning behind it. Offering historical perspective will be former Mayor Susan Payne, who will discuss the lake’s history and the efforts made to reopen it to the public during her time in office.

Dr. Stephanie Hernandez, who previously served as acting city manager, will address the direction she gave during her tenure to seek funding for the lake, including a lodger’s tax proposal intended to support its operation.

The economic stakes of the debate will be represented by the owner of Bonito Bait and Tackle, who will speak to the significance of the lake and the livelihoods tied to its continued existence. Rounding out the panel are Commissioner Warren Robinson, who will discuss his role in the debate as an elected official

The forum begins at 6 p.m. and is hosted by Alamogordo Town News. It will be broadcast live on KALH Radio and streamed on YouTube for those unable to attend in person. Organizers are billing the event as a civil conversation and encourage community members to attend.

item.title: John Lynn Sheffield Obituary
item.description:
John Lynn Sheffield

John Lynn Sheffield, who explored the canyons of New Mexico and Colorado, passed through the veil of this life and began his journey exploring the heavens above on August 18, 2026.

John’s tremendous heart and gentle spirit always welcomed everyone he met. He greeted people with a big handshake, a smile, and an instant sense of friendship. John was a very generous soul, always ready to accept any hike, race, adventure, or challenge offered by family or friends.

John was born in Albuquerque, New Mexico, to his parents, Leonard and Sarah Jane Sheffield, on February 21, 1956. Raised in the mountains of southern New Mexico, John thoroughly enjoyed hiking and cycling, with many favorite trails in and around Colorado Springs. Being in nature fed his soul.

John graduated from Alamogordo Senior High in 1974. He worked in his father’s furniture business where he developed an appreciation for small business and entrepreneurship. After graduating from Oral Roberts University, John went on to build a life in business, owning and operating a furniture store, a pipe and supply business, and a real estate business, as well as serving in management at the Glen Eyrie Castle Conference Center.

John’s greatest love was his family. He is survived by his lifelong love, Teri Lea Sheffield; his son Jason Sheffield (Tiffany); his daughter Kristin Sheffield (Morgan); and his daughter, Irena Sheffield. He was a grandfather to his four beloved grandchildren, Kadence, Jonas, Evelyn, and Soren. John also enjoyed the love and friendship of his brother, Larry Sheffield (Tara), his sister, Janet Evans (John), as well as his wonderful in-laws and nine nieces and three nephews.

John left behind a legacy of faith, sincere kindness and love for others, a commitment to studying biblical and historical subjects, and countless friendships. He will also be remembered for his humility, his encouragement to so many, and, especially, his bravery in fighting the many challenges he experienced throughout his life.

Colorado Springs was John’s home, where he built a life surrounded by family and friends. He also made regular visits to Alamogordo to manage the family real estate business. His love for history, reading, music, conversation, and storytelling was all part of his wonderful personality.

A private celebration of life will be held by John’s family, and in lieu of flowers, please plant a tree, be kind to a stranger, or stop to watch a sunset and think of John.

item.title: Sounds of Silence from Sunspot
item.description:
Both the U.S. Forest Service and the National Science Foundation are declining comment about ongoing work at Sunspot Solar Observatory.

In last week’s announcement that mercury has been removed from the Dunn Solar Telescope — and that it must be demolished because of decades of smaller leaks — both NSF and the Forest Service stated that “the Forest Service will continue to explore potential future opportunities that create public value and honor the site’s long-standing legacy. As ideas begin to take shape, the Lincoln National Forest plans to engage local partners and interested stakeholders to better understand community priorities and interests.”

Alamogordo Town News responded with several questions about a preliminary timeline for a contract and demolition, and whether new instruments that had been installed just before the leak had been removed.

“NSF declines comment,” was the response from media affairs specialist Cassandra Eichner. “We will issue additional updates as new information becomes available.”

A follow-up request not for an update but an explanation of a past decision — why Sunspot was not listed in the National Register of Historic Places — was ignored.

The Forest Service is equally reticent. ATN asked for details about which facilities might be available for repurposing, remediation before a new operator moves in, the comment period, and how it planned on communicating results to the public.

“All inquires on this topic can be submitted to NSF_Sac_Peak@nsf.gov,” was the anonymous answer. Past inquiries to that address have not been answered.

“Community organizations or individuals who would like to stay informed about future discussions are welcome to contact the Lincoln National Forest at ReImagineSunspotNM@usda.gov,” the joint announcement said. “NSF and the Forest Service will continue to provide updates as the remediation process moves forward.”

However, an ATN inquiry to that e-mail address has not been acknowledged, and NSF has only provided three updates: that the leak occurred, that the Dunn would be decommissioned, and the most recent announcements that the mercury was removed.

Sunspot Community Center has met with Cloudcorft, Alamogordo, and Oterio County commissions to brief them on possible repurposing Sunspot with options including dark skies “astrotourism” and a science education park addressing forestry and astronomy.

Note: Dave Dooling is a veteran areospace writer and educator who lives in High Rolls New Mexico. He is retired as the education director at the New Mexico Museum of Space history, and now runs The Traveling Gizmo Show.

item.title: Commentary: How Much More Can the Mountains Take? Why Regional Collaboration is Important
item.description:
Fire, flood, a dark racetrack, a soon to demolished observatory and now a fence around Bonito Lake. Our mountain towns are losing their attractions one decision at a time, no one is keeping the regional ledger, and Alamogordo is downstream of every loss.

Otero & Lincoln Counties, New Mexico- There is a shop owner in midtown Ruidoso whose wholesale warehouse filled with floodwater last July. He told a public radio reporter this spring that his business is done between June and September, and that it is done with the racing crowd. This summer there was no racing crowd. For the first time since 1947, the grandstand at Ruidoso Downs sat empty on Labor Day weekend, and the All American Futurity, the richest quarter horse race in the world, was run in Albuquerque.

That is one business in one town in the region. Multiply it across two counties, and you begin to see the shape of what has happened to the Sacramento Mountains economy since June 2024. The region has taken a beating that no single mayor, commission, agency or business owner can see whole, because each blow has landed from a different direction and been decided by a different set of hands.

Lay the losses end to end and the picture is sobering.

In June 2024, the South Fork and Salt fires burned roughly 17,000 acres and about 1,400 structures and forced the evacuation of the entire village of Ruidoso at the start of peak season. The burn scars have driven every flood since.

In July 2024 and again in July 2025, those burn scars sent floodwater through the village. On July 8, 2025, the Rio Ruidoso crested at a record 20 feet; three people died, including two children, and emergency crews carried out 50 to 60 swift-water rescues. Ruidoso was placed under nearly a dozen flash flood emergencies in 2025 alone. According to the village's own financial reports, lodgers' tax revenue fell almost 30 percent from fiscal year 2024 to fiscal year 2025, and taxable receipts for accommodation and food service fell about 19 percent.

On January 19, 2026, Ruidoso Downs announced there would be no horse racing this year, the first time in more than 80 years. An engineering study concluded the site cannot be adequately protected from flooding even with the mitigation work proposed, on-site and upstream. Village officials say the track supports hundreds of jobs. Midtown merchants say their June-to-September season is the racing crowd.

On January 5, 2026, liquid mercury was discovered inside the Dunn Solar Telescope at Sunspot, eighteen miles south of Cloudcroft. On February 25, the National Science Foundation announced it will remove the mercury, demolish the tower and restore the site. The visitor center is closed indefinitely, ending a destination that drew science tourists and school groups up U.S. 82 for more than fifty years.

And on August 25, 2026, Alamogordo's city manager Robert Stockwell asked the Alamogordo City Commission to end public fishing access at Bonito Lake and spend up to $1 million on security fencing, two summers after a twelve-year closure finally ended. The Commission tabled the item to September 22. It is the only entry on this list that is a choice rather than a disaster.

There is some good news mixed in, and it should not be ignored. Ruidoso's retail sales held roughly steady through the last fiscal year. Lodgers' tax collections through the first eight months of this fiscal year ran a few percent ahead of last year's depressed numbers. Contour Airlines began flying Ruidoso to Denver in May. Ruidoso was named the country's best small-town cultural scene by USA Today readers for the second year running, and the XTERRA World Championship has committed to the village through 2028. People in Ruidoso are not quitting. Their retail is down seven or eight percent, one civic leader said this spring, not fifty or sixty.

But seven or eight percent, sustained for three summers, on top of a lost racing season, on top of a demolished observatory, on top of insurance premiums and rebuilding costs and a monsoon season that the village spent the spring preparing residents for with flood workshops and a redrawn floodplain map, is not resilience. It is attrition. A community and a region can absorb one disaster. It cannot indefinitely absorb a disaster and then a series of quiet closures that each seem reasonable to the people making them.

It is tempting, from the Tularosa Basin floor, to view all of this as Lincoln County's problem. It is not. Alamogordo is the gateway to these mountains. U.S. 70 and U.S. 54 carry the families from El Paso, Las Cruces, Lubbock and Midland who make up the region's visitor base, and the vast majority of them pass through this city to get there. They fuel up on White Sands Boulevard. They eat breakfast at Our Country Kitchen on New York Avenue and shop at Our Little Country Store, Victoria and Roadrunner Galleria and they eat dinner on White Sands Blvd while in town. They stop at the Museum of Space History and White Sands National Park on the way in and buy pistachios on the way out. When Ruidoso has a bad summer, Alamogordo's restaurants, motels, gas stations and downtown merchants have a bad summer with it. It is a quieter one, harder to see in any single ledger, but it is real, having owned businesses downtown this journalist has seen first hand the ebb and flow tourism can have on a financial ledger.

Cloudcroft sits in Otero County, not Lincoln, and Sunspot was on our side of the line. Every visitor the Dunn telescope drew for half a century drove through Alamogordo twice. Cloudcroft's leaders are now asking the federal government to at least slow the demolition of the remaining buildings while they look for a new use. They should not be doing that alone. 

See related article at Sounds of Silence from Sunspot by ATN Science and Space Reporter David Dooling

Every closure on the list was decided by people who were not asked to weigh what the region had already lost.

Here is the pattern. The National Science Foundation weighed the cost of a mercury cleanup against the value of a telescope superseded by a newer one in Hawaii, and chose demolition. A racetrack owner weighed an engineering report against another flooded season, and chose Albuquerque. A city manager weighed a parks fund against complaints about mud in a parking lot, and chose a fence. Each decision was made by someone with a narrow mandate and a specific balance sheet. Not one of them was made by anyone whose job it was to ask: what does this region look like when all of these things are gone at once?

No one holds that job. That is the real problem, and it is the one the mountain communities and the basin city can actually fix.

Of everything on that ledger, Bonito Lake is the only item that is not a disaster, a federal decision or an act of God. It is a recommendation, from a city manager Robert Stockwell to seven elected commissioners, that can be declined.

The lake reopened to anglers in August 2024, after twelve years and more than $8 million in restoration, under a prepaid agreement with the state wildlife department that stocked it with trout. The Legislature approved $250,000 this spring, at the city's own request, for shoreline and day-use improvements. Fencing it now, at a cost of up to $1 million, would take one more attraction off the regional map in the same year the racetrack and the observatory came off it, and would do so by choice, with state money on the table to keep it open.

The city manager's argument is that Bonito's visitors spend their money in Lincoln County, not Alamogordo. Read in isolation, that has a certain accounting logic. Read against this year's ledger, it is exactly the thinking that has hollowed out the region: every jurisdiction protecting its own column while the shared economy that feeds all of them shrinks. Alamogordo cannot expect Ruidoso to send visitors down the hill if Alamogordo will not keep its own lake open on the hill.

The Sacramento Mountains and the Tularosa Basin are one tourism economy divided among two counties, four municipalities, a sovereign tribal nation, a national forest, a national park and an Air Force base. Visitors do not experience those boundaries. Our governments should stop acting as though they do. Concretely:

How much more can the local economy take? The honest answer is that no one knows, because no one is counting. The racetrack owner counted his flood risk. The NSF counted its mercury. The city manager counted his parks fund. The merchants in midtown Ruidoso and on New York Avenue are counting the empty tables, and they are the only ones counting the whole thing.

Alamogordo's commissioners will vote on Sept. 22 on the one item on this year's ledger that is still within local control. They should keep the lake open — not only because the money is there and the plan is adopted, but because a region that has lost this much in two years cannot afford to hand away anything else voluntarily. And when that vote is done, someone in this city and someone in that village should pick up the phone and start building the regional table that should have existed before the first fire.

That table gets its first test tonight.

The Alamogordo Town News Kalhradio.org Voices of Alamogordo community forum on the future of Bonito Lake is tonight, Tuesday, September 1, at 6 p.m. at Otero Arts, 1118 Indiana Avenue, Alamogordo. The panel will include City Manager Robert Stockwell, a sitting city commissioner, a former mayor, a former city manager, representatives of businesses near Bonito Lake, and representatives from the Village of Ruidoso. For the first time since the fencing proposal surfaced, the people who own the lake, the people who manage it, and the people whose livelihoods depend on it will be in the same room.

The forum is free and open to the public. Bring your questions. For those who cannot attend in person, the event will be streamed live on the Alamogordo Town News Facebook page and on the KALHRadio.org YouTube channel.

item.title: Voices of Alamogordo KALHRadio.org Packed House at Community Forum as Stockwell Backs Off Bonito Lake Fence Proposal
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — A crowd filled a community forum this week to weigh in on the future of Bonito Lake, where Alamogordo City Manager Bob Stockwell announced he will walk back his earlier recommendation to close the lake to the public and will instead present a five-point compromise plan to the city commission on September 22 — one that keeps the lake open for fishing and limits fencing to the dam area only.

The turnout underscored how deeply the issue resonates across the region. Three city commissioners and Mayor Sharon McDonald attended from the audience, alongside commissioners Warren Robinson, Al Hernandez, and Stephen Burnett. The panel featured former Mayor Susan Payne, former City Manager Dr. Stephanie Hernandez, small business owners, and the mayors of both Ruidoso and Ruidoso Downs. County commission candidate Alan Gonzalez and candidate Evan Ross joined the dialogue, and commenting from the audience were representatives of New Mexico Fish and Wildlife, the county CEO, and other officials. Several hundred more citizens tuned in to the livestream.

https://www.youtube.com/live/MW0TxL89yQM?si=t9i-0zFcxKyKxlKh

A reversal, but not a retreat

Reading from prepared remarks — something he acknowledged he rarely does — Stockwell traced his history with the lake back to 1992, when he first managed the city and concluded that the lake’s role as the single best water source in the city’s inventory had to come before recreation. He noted the lake was already about 40 percent silted in during the 1990s, a problem that went unaddressed until the devastating 2023 fires and debris flows forced its closure. After restoration, water began flowing consistently to the city again in 2026.

Stockwell was at times defiant in defending his original recommendation to close the lake entirely, stressing that the detention basins, ponds, and drainage systems built to intercept debris have left surrounding areas hazardous — former parking areas, he said, are now subject to mud flows that would have trapped vehicles during this summer’s storms. His comments returned again and again to a single theme: the lake was purchased in the 1950s as a water source, and protecting the city’s drinking water comes first.

But citing constructive public input and interest from state officials — including Senator Jim Tompson, who has agreed to convene legislative colleagues and state agencies — Stockwell outlined the five recommendations he will bring to the commission:

1. Direct the city manager to open discussions with the state, Otero County, Lincoln County, and Ruidoso officials on options that preserve Alamogordo’s water supply while exploring compatible recreation at the lake and surrounding areas.

2. Continue construction of the remaining debris-flow protection projects.

3. Construct required security fencing around the dam structure and ancillary facilities only — not the lake itself.

4. Maintain the status quo allowing public access for fishing.

5. Post additional signage advising visitors that the lake is a primary municipal water source and that anyone entering city property does so at their own risk.

He also proposed a six-month deadline to report back to the commission on the results of the regional discussions.

Payne pushes back on tone and priorities

Former Mayor Susan Payne offered the evening’s sharpest criticism of Stockwell’s approach, saying she was “stunned” that full closure was ever suggested and questioning, through her comments, his commitment to community and lifestyle programs. While she called the new proposal an improvement over what was presented at the earlier commission meeting, she argued the city should have anticipated the access problems.

Payne framed the issue as one of quality of life, comparing the lake to city parks that require maintenance but would never be fenced off or shut down. She pointed to the 12 years the lake sat closed, during which, she said, an entire generation lost the chance to fish there and make memories — something she does not want repeated. She also credited city employee Dave Nunley with the idea that saved the lake from renewed debris damage, and urged both sides to approach the September meeting with open minds and a willingness to bend.

Business owners see regional dollars at stake

This journalist a former downtown  business owner who ran Roadrunner Emporium on New York Avenue told the crowd that 70 percent of his revenue came from tourists, many of them passing through Alamogordo on their way to Lincoln County or Cloudcroft — evidence, he said, of the direct gains from regional tourism collaboration.

The Bonito Bait and Tackle business owners with a property near the lake, described buying burn-scar land six years ago, betting on the area’s recovery, and launching a bait stand with his children for $400 that has grown into a profitable business gaining momentum weekly. He praised Stockwell’s revised plan as an excellent compromise and urged Alamogordo’s leaders to invest in the lake’s recreational infrastructure and regional partnerships.

Regional leaders offer help

Dr. Stephanie Hernandez defended the process itself, saying the commission’s decision to table the original recommendation and gather public input was exactly how government should work, with no malice on either side. The core question, she said, is a policy decision for the commission: is Bonito Lake a reservoir only, or a reservoir and a recreation facility? She also singled out Commissioner P. Chavis, whose crew camped at the lake during the fires and completed protective ponds in a matter of days, crediting them with saving the lake outright.

The mayor of Ruidoso emphasized that his village’s recovery from the McBride fire, the South Fork fire, and successive flooding was only possible through help from Alamogordo, Tularosa, Roswell, and the state — and pledged the same cooperation in return. He described how Ruidoso manages its own reservoir lakes as drinking water sources first while still allowing recreation: regular water testing, no gasoline engines, kayaks permitted, and events like XTERRA and Ironman that have generated significant economic activity. Insuring a lake, he added, costs no more than insuring a skateboard park. State Representative Harley Vincent, he noted, was already on the phone with senators about a path forward.

The Ruidoso Downs mayor and Lincoln County officials echoed the offer to meet with Alamogordo’s city manager and pursue a regional approach.

What happens next

The commission takes up Stockwell’s revised recommendations at its September 22 meeting, public comments are encouraged. If adopted, the plan would launch six months of formal talks among city, county, state, and federal partners on a collaboration agreement to keep the lake open for public recreation — and on funding to maintain and enhance a property that Wednesday’s crowd made clear the region considers far more than a reservoir.

item.title: Tularosa Approves Land Purchase for Backup Water Supply as River Flows Decline
item.description:
TULAROSA, N.M. — Facing a shrinking river and the threat of future water shortages, the Village of Tularosa’s board of trustees has approved the purchase of an 84-acre tract south of town, clearing the way for a supplemental groundwater treatment facility officials hope to have running by late 2028.

The decision, made after a series of public meetings and a formal hearing, marks a major step in a project the village has been planning since 2022. Tularosa currently depends on a surface water treatment plant fed by the Rio Tularosa, but hydrologic data from 2001 through 2024 shows a steady decline in summer river flows — precisely when demand from irrigation and household use peaks.

“Failure to act risks repeated water shortages and emergency restrictions,” officials told residents, pointing to recent shortages in the village and similar struggles in communities across New Mexico, including the Rio Grande Valley.

An Old Well, New Technology

At the heart of the plan is the Monazuma well, drilled in the 1950s, which the village intends to redevelop as the source for a new reverse osmosis desalination plant. Groundwater from the well carries roughly 2,250 parts per million of total dissolved solids — more than four times the EPA’s secondary drinking water standard, though not unusual for New Mexico. The RO system’s membrane filtration would bring that figure below 5 ppm, producing what engineers described as pristine potable water.

Reverse osmosis is a decades-old technology that has been continually refined, and the Tularosa plant will include two redundant treatment units so operations can continue during maintenance or if one unit runs into problems. Because the process is energy-intensive — one of the chief drawbacks of desalination — the village will install solar panels to offset power consumption and keep the treated water affordable.

But the process comes with a catch: about 18 percent of the water pumped will be rejected as brine, a highly saline waste stream with concentrations around 13,000 ppm that will grow saltier — past 100,000 ppm — as it concentrates over time.

Evaporation Ponds Drive Land Purchase

Managing that brine is the reason for the land acquisition. The village plans to dedicate roughly 25 to 30 acres of the new parcel to lined evaporation ponds, built with polyethylene liners, six-foot water depths, berms, fencing, and state-required monitoring wells to guard against groundwater contamination. Officials said natural, sun-driven evaporation is far cheaper than energy- and chemical-intensive disposal alternatives, but it requires a large contiguous tract close to town — which drove the selection of this particular property.

The facility will operate under stricter regulations than a typical wastewater treatment pond, officials said. Both the treatment plant and the ponds sit outside the waterway itself and will not affect the Rio Tularosa channel. Down the road, the system could eventually tie into aquifer storage and recharge programs to improve long-term sustainability.

Residents Voice Concerns

Public hearings drew questions and concerns from residents, particularly those with private wells near the Monazuma well who worried that increased pumping could draw down their own water supplies and hurt pecan and pistachio operations. Village officials acknowledged some unpredictability until pumping actually begins, but noted the state regulates withdrawal volumes and conducts impact reviews.

Neighbors of the proposed pond site raised questions about contamination, mosquitoes, windborne salt particles, and property values. Officials responded that the ponds will be lined, fenced, monitored, and odorless, though they conceded there is little precedent for evaporation ponds near residences, making effects on property values difficult to predict.

Water Rights Cut Looms

A significant legal hurdle remains: converting the well’s water rights from agricultural to municipal use. The Monazuma well currently holds 210 acre-feet of agricultural rights, but state conversion rules are expected to cut that to about 70 acre-feet — a two-thirds reduction that limits how much the facility can contribute. Officials stressed the plant is intended to supplement, not replace, the cheaper surface water supply, and it will not fully cover peak summer irrigation demand.

Costs and Timeline

The project’s capital cost, including the land, is estimated at $4 million to $5 million, with annual pumping and treatment costs projected to add $30,000 to $40,000 when running at full capacity. Grants and state funding have supported the design phase to date.

Construction is expected to begin by mid-2027 and last about 15 months, putting the facility on track to deliver water by late 2028.

item.title: Commentary: The Future of Bonito Lake Is a Policy Decision
item.description:
A commentary by Dr. Stephanie Hernandez…

I recently wrote about what I believe should be the priorities of a City Commission. After the budget, my second priority was policy and direction. The current discussion surrounding Bonito Lake is a good example of why that responsibility matters and how the different pieces of municipal government are supposed to work together.

In our form of government, the City Manager works for the City Commission. The manager's responsibility is to provide the Commission with the best professional advice based available information, staff recommendations, financial considerations, operational realities and professional judgment.

City staff report through the City Manager. Department directors are the subject-matter experts in their areas, and their knowledge is invaluable. But regardless of where an idea begins, with a director, an employee, the City Manager, or citizen, the decision to move forward belongs to the City Manager. Staff then has the responsibility to present and support the recommendation and bring forward.

The Commission has a different role. Commissioners must consider the professional advice of staff, but they must also listen to the citizens they represent. Sometimes those two perspectives will align perfectly. Sometimes they do not. The Commission weighs both and establishes policy and direction.

That brings us to Bonito Lake. In 2024, the City Commission approved a master plan that included a direction for Bonito Lake. That approval gave staff the roadmap.

Master plans should never be treated as documents that are written, approved and placed permanently on a shelf. They are a living document. Conditions change. Costs change. Opportunities change. Community priorities can change.

The current discussion is not necessarily about whether someone was right or wrong in 2024 or whether someone is right or wrong today. It is an opportunity for the Commission to decide whether the policy direction it previously established remains the direction the community wants.

The fundamental policy question is simple: Is Bonito Lake strictly a municipal water reservoir, or is it primarily a water reservoir with recreation as an important secondary use?

That is a policy decision.

I believe the Commission made a smart decision when it tabled the item rather than immediately taking final action. Tabling gives commissioners time to obtain additional information, but more importantly, it gives the citizens an opportunity to tell them what you want.

When I began receiving text messages about the issue, I went back and watched the meeting. I am not surprised by the public response.

When we filled Bonito Lake, I received calls from people across New Mexico asking when fishing and camping would reopen. We were not ready to reopen the campgrounds but believed there were things we could do to allow day-fishing.

When the lake was stocked and we were preparing to open fishing in May, the fire interrupted those plans. Once the fire was contained, the calls started again: When are you opening Bonito for fishing?

Former City Manager Rick Holden received inquiries as well, including calls from legislators all over New Mexico. I continued receiving questions about when additional camping opportunities might return.

People have an emotional attachment to it the recreational value extends beyond Alamogordo.

Where things stood when I left

I want to be particularly careful here. I am no longer involved in City operations, and I do not know what has occurred since I left. I cannot speak to administrative decisions. I can only speak to where things were, to the best of my recollection, when I was City Manager.

Parks and Recreation Director Bass was following the master plan because that was the approved direction.

I remember discussions about beginning with lower-cost, more natural camping opportunities such as tent camping and gradually developing additional recreational opportunities, potentially including an RV area below the lake. I do not remember every detail of the plan. What I do remember clearly was the philosophy: we did not have enough money to do everything, but that did not mean we could do nothing. That was my overall concept regarding every department. We had to keep moving.

Start with what we could reasonably afford. Improve it over time. Follow the master plan. Work with stakeholders and pursue partnerships that could help stretch limited City resources. At the time, outdoor recreation and tourism were priorities at the state level, creating opportunities to work with state agencies on grants or partnerships to move the master plan forward over time.

Truthfully, that is how we approached quality-of-life improvements throughout the City.

For Bonito, my focus was finding a recurring funding source through lodgers' tax. Director Bass, Erik and others were working on different pieces of the overall plan. One of the strengths of the City's department directors was their passion in their field. As City Manager, I depended on them to identify opportunities and bring forward solutions.

I recalled the $250,000 ICIP funding that has recently been discussed. We made a deliberate effort to place quality-of-life projects into the City's capital planning when possible. That approach helped fund improvements throughout our parks, zoo and recreational facilities.

I remember Director Bass had discussions involving New Mexico Game and Fish and know that I approved moving certain discussions forward and a review of the proposed contract. The directors were able to give feedback. What happened after that, I cannot say.

I had forgotten There was also a contractor who was expected to complete additional work around the stairways. Again, I left before that process was completed, so I cannot responsibly say where that work stands today.

Those are items the current administration can answer much better than I can.

What about the security concern?

One massive concern raised by staff deserves serious treatment. Protecting a municipal drinking water source is always a legitimate concern.Security was something I worried about constantly as City Manager.

One of my recurring nightmares was whether we were prepared for a major train derailment involving hazardous materials. The railroad runs directly through our community and business district. The chiefs were probably tired of my constant questions about scenarios I had developed in my mind and whether we were prepared for them. Some were low probability but potentially high consequence events. I wanted us thinking about those risks before an emergency occurred, not during one. That is how emergency management works. You do not ignore a risk simply because it is unlikely. The same principle should apply at Bonito.

Identifying a risk does not automatically dictate one particular policy response. Security should be layered because no single security measure can make a critical water source completely secure. A fence can establish a boundary, discourage casual entry and delay unauthorized access. Those are legitimate benefits. But a chain-link fence by itself should not be confused with a comprehensive security system.

Protecting critical infrastructure generally requires multiple safeguards, including controlled access, monitoring, cameras, alarms, water quality testing, communications, operational procedures and an emergency response plan.

Bonito already has monitoring infrastructure, including SCADA and the City had been working on expanding communications and monitoring capabilities.

The approximately 80-mile distance between Bonito Lake and Alamogordo should also be discussed accurately. Distance does not eliminate the risk of contamination, and I would never suggest that it does. However, the conveyance and treatment process can provide something extremely valuable in an emergency: time. That is a much stronger security conversation than simply asking whether there is a fence.

There may also be another part of the solution: people. One reason I advocated changing the state lodgers' tax law so Alamogordo could use a portion of its tourism-related revenue for Bonito Lake operations.

If that legislation passed and then reestablished in Alamogordo, 60% of that recurring revenue could potentially support operations.

One option worth considering would be an on-site employee or caretaker presence at Bonito Lake, similar in concept to the landfill. An employee presence would not replace cameras, alarms, testing or other security measures. It would add another layer. Someone regularly on the property can identify problems, report suspicious activity, address maintenance issues, communicate quickly with Alamogordo and initiate established emergency procedures while additional personnel are responding.

That improves recreation and security at the same time.

Now the decision belongs to the Commission and to the public.

Staff has an obligation to tell the Commission what it believes is operationally best. The City Manager has an obligation to evaluate that information and make a professional recommendation.

Citizens have every right to say, we understand the recommendation, but this community values something different. Then the Commission has to weigh both.

That is not government dysfunction. That is exactly how representative local government is supposed to work and aligns with my overall discussion on priorities

The question before Alamogordo should not be framed as water versus recreation. Protecting our water supply must remain the first priority.

The better question is whether those two purposes can responsibly coexist:

Bonito Lake first as an essential water resource, and second as a recreational and quality-of-life asset belonging to the people of Alamogordo.

In 2024, the Commission gave staff one direction. Today, the Commission has the obligation to reaffirm it, modify it or establish a new one.

Because ultimately, staff recommends, the City Manager manages, the Commission sets policy and the Commission answers to you.

Dear Doctor,

Sincerely,

A Feller Who’s Seen This Rodeo Before

item.title: State Police Investigate Fatal Dog Mauling in Santa Rosa; Dogs’ Owner Charged
item.description:
SANTA ROSA, N.M. — A 73-year-old man died Friday after being attacked by two dogs outside his home on Tapia Road, and the dogs’ owner now faces a felony charge, the New Mexico State Police said.

The State Police Investigations Bureau is leading the inquiry into the Aug. 28 attack that killed Randy Wade. The Santa Rosa Police Department and State Police officers were the first to respond before bureau agents took over the case.

Investigators said Wade was outside his home when two dogs belonging to James Campbell, 52, attacked him near a shed. The attack was determined to be unprovoked.

Campbell and a woman were staying at Wade’s home at the time. According to investigators, the woman was outside when she witnessed the attack and called for Campbell, who was inside. Campbell came out and secured the dogs in an enclosure, then moved Wade to the front porch, where Wade was found to be deceased. The woman called 911.

During an interview with investigators, Campbell acknowledged that he knew his dogs had previously been deemed vicious. Investigators also learned the dogs, both pit bull mixes, had reportedly been involved in an earlier attack and had recently been released from an animal shelter.

Campbell has been charged with Dangerous Dog (Death of a Person), a third-degree felony under New Mexico law.

The investigation remains active, State Police said.

item.title: Area Volleyball Roundup: Lady Tigers Fall to Silver; Tularosa Picks Up First Win
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — The Alamogordo Lady Tigers came up short at home Tuesday night, falling to Silver in straight sets, 25-19, 25-17, 25-21.

Silver controlled the tempo throughout the match, holding off every Alamogordo push. The Lady Tigers battled to keep the third set close but couldn’t string together enough points down the stretch to extend the match.

The loss drops Alamogordo to 1-2 on the young season. The Lady Tigers won’t have long to regroup — they head south this weekend to compete in the Jane Leupold Sweet 16 Tournament in Las Cruces on Friday and Saturday, where they’ll face a deep field of competition.

Tularosa Earns First Victory of the Season

The Tularosa Lady Cats notched their first win of the year, sweeping Socorro in three hard-fought sets, 26-24, 25-18, 26-24.

It wasn’t easy. Two of the three sets went to extra points, with Tularosa closing out both the first and third frames 26-24. The Lady Cats showed poise in the tight moments, finding a way to finish sets that could have gone either way.

Tularosa improves to 1-4 and will look to build momentum when it hosts Mescalero Apache next Tuesday.

Lady Chiefs Still Searching for First Win

Mescalero Apache dropped a four-set decision to Alamo Navajo, falling to 0-4 on the season.

The Lady Chiefs will get a chance to break into the win column this weekend at the Gateway Christian Tournament in Roswell, which runs Friday and Saturday, before traveling to Tularosa next week.

Cloudcroft Splits at Hatch Valley Tournament

The Cloudcroft Lady Bears went 1-1 at the Hatch Valley Tournament, evening their record at 3-3.

Cloudcroft opened with a straight-set loss to Cimarron, 25-18, 25-22, 25-23, in a match that tightened with every set — the Lady Bears fell just two points short in the final frame.

They responded emphatically in their second match, dismantling Reserve in three lopsided sets, 25-11, 25-17, 25-7. The Lady Bears’ serving and net play overwhelmed Reserve from the opening whistle, including a dominant 25-7 closing set.

Cloudcroft gets a quick rematch with Reserve on Friday, this time on the road.

item.title: From Parole Officer to the Bench: Lujan Grisham Appoints Joseph Cutts to Otero County Magistrate Court
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — A longtime New Mexico corrections officer is moving from supervising criminal cases to presiding over them after Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham appointed Joseph Cutts to the Otero County Magistrate Court.

Cutts will take over Division 2 following the resignation of Judge Albert R. Greene III. His appointment begins Sept. 12 and will last until the next general election.

The appointment caps an unusual path to the bench. Cutts defeated Greene, the incumbent, in the June 2 Republican primary, and Greene stepped down after the loss. Because no other candidates filed for the seat, Cutts will run unopposed in the Nov. 3 general election — meaning the governor’s appointment effectively installs him in a job voters had already signaled would be his.

The Division 2 race was one of only a handful of contested contests on Otero County’s primary ballot this year, in a county where Republican primaries are frequently decisive. Magistrate judges in New Mexico handle misdemeanor cases and preliminary hearings, serving as many residents’ first — and often only — point of contact with the court system.

Cutts brings more than a decade of criminal justice experience to the role, though from the enforcement side rather than the courtroom. He has served as a senior adult probation and parole officer with the New Mexico Corrections Department since 2012, supervising offenders after conviction. He also teaches criminal justice at New Mexico State University Alamogordo.

His academic credentials run through the same field. Cutts earned an Associate of Applied Science in criminal justice from NMSU Alamogordo, a bachelor’s degree in criminal justice from NMSU in Las Cruces, and a Master of Science in criminal justice from the University of Oklahoma.

Unlike district court judgeships, New Mexico magistrate judges are not required to be licensed attorneys in most jurisdictions, opening the bench to candidates with broader criminal justice backgrounds like Cutts. 

Greene’s departure ends a relatively short but effective tenure on the court. Greene had a respectable reputation as an attorney prior to his appointment. He was appointed to the Otero County bench by Lujan Grisham in 2023, filling a vacancy left by the resignation of Judge Michael Ryan Suggs. Before joining the magistrate court, Greene worked as a domestic relations hearing officer with the Twelfth Judicial District Court and as a senior Children’s Court attorney with the New Mexico Children, Youth and Families Department.

Cutts is expected to stand for the seat in the Nov. 3 general election, where he faces no opposition.

A Good man. Congrats Judge Cutts!

item.title: Eight Plein Air Artists to Open at Otero Artspace This Friday
item.description:
Alamogordo, NM — Otero Arts will open a new exhibition, “Eight Plein Air Artists,” with a public reception this Friday, September 4, from 5 to 7 p.m. at the Otero Artspace, 1118 Indiana Avenue at 12th Street.

The show features work by eight area painters: Anne Aleshire, Janet Amtmann, Lyn Canham, Rand Carlson, Deidre Kindthistle, Sue Nichols, Julie Ford Oliver, and Diana Powell. Their paintings were created on site at locations across the region, including Bent, Tularosa Falls, High Rolls, Alamogordo, La Luz, White Sands National Park, Nichols Ranch, and the Alamogordo Zoo. Media represented in the show include acrylic, oil, watercolor, pastel, and gouache.

Plein air painting — a portrait of the landscape in natural light — is a genre developed by painters in the 1800s who left their dark studios behind, carrying easels and tubes of paint outdoors.

Most of the artists in the show began painting together in October 2025 in a plein air workshop taught by Santa Fe artist Anita Louise West. Since then, the group has met one day a week to paint “en plein air.” Many have practiced the craft for years, painting throughout New Mexico as well as on trips abroad, in Alaska, and elsewhere.

Visitors to the exhibition will find anecdotes displayed alongside the paintings, describing what drew each artist to the subject of the piece. Kindthistle’s “The Pool,” for example, began as a tribute to David Hockney and became a farewell portrait: after 30 years of offering citizens a friendly respite from summer’s heat, the city pool is slated for demolition, to be replaced by a modern natatorium.

For Amtmann, who came to ranch life as a young woman, plein air painting is a way of preserving a quietly vanishing world. For decades she has painted what surrounds her in the Sacramento Mountains — the horses and cattle, the orchards and wildflowers, the storms and long evening light, and the people who make their lives on that ground.

“Eight Plein Air Artists” runs through September 26. The Otero Artspace gallery is open Thursday through Sunday, 1 to 4 p.m.

This October, Otero Arts will offer its fourth plein air workshop, again taught by Anita Louise West. Sign-up details are available at oteroarts.org. Anyone interested in joining the plein air painters on Thursdays may contact janet.amtmann@gmail.com.

The exhibit is supported by New Mexico Arts, the Department of Cultural Affairs, and the National Endowment for the Arts.

item.title: Changing the Narrative on Suicide’ brings walk, workshops and mayoral proclamation to Alameda Park Saturday
item.description:
Alamogordo N. M- Alamogordo residents will gather at Alameda Park this Saturday, Sept. 5, from 8 to 11 a.m. for “Changing the Narrative on Suicide,” a free community event offering a morning of movement, resources, and open conversation about suicide prevention.

Mayor Sharon McDonald will deliver remarks and an official proclamation, and speakers will share how suicide has affected their lives. An open space will give community members a chance to tell their own stories, and more than 13 local organizations — including 100% Otero and The Toy Train Depot — will be on hand with booths and resources.

Fitness instructors from around the community will lead free workshops throughout the morning. According to the schedule posted on the Chamber of Commerce’s community calendar, yoga begins at 8 a.m., followed by tai chi at 8:30, Zumba at 9, MixxedFit at 9:30, belly dancing at 10, and dance fitness at 10:30.

The event is hosted by the Otero Youth Empowerment Project and the Otero Humanists, whose co-founder and director, math and computer science tutor Spencer Bond, began organizing it about two months ago after losing someone close to him to suicide. What started as one person’s idea quickly grew into a citywide effort, with organizations, instructors, and volunteers signing on to help.

“Suicide prevention is so much bigger than any one of us,” Bond said. “This event never would have come together without the help of the community.”

Nani Lawrence, president of the Otero Humanists, helped shape the morning’s lineup of activities, with an emphasis on hope rather than heaviness.

“When you talk about suicide, it can be very much doom and gloom as it is,” Lawrence said. “However, our event focuses on the things that you look forward to that might make someone realize that they have all these great things. I think that it will provide a lot of hope.”

Organizers say the event is designed for everyone — those who have lost someone to suicide, those who have struggled themselves, and anyone who wants to support their neighbors. Families are welcome, and no registration is required.

“Changing the Narrative on Suicide” will be held Saturday, Sept. 5, from 8 to 11 a.m. at Alameda Park in Alamogordo. Admission is free. For more information, contact Spencer Bond at 575-339-4046.

item.title: Mayor McDonald Says Public Response to Bonito Lake Conversation ‘Remarkable’
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — Facing an outpouring of public support for Bonito Lake, City Manager Brian Stockwell announced he will recommend a change of direction to the Alamogordo City Commission on Sept. 22 — one that keeps the lake open for fishing while regional talks explore its recreational future.

Stockwell made the commitment at a community forum hosted at Otero Arts by Alamogordo Town News and KALHRadio.org, which drew a large and diverse crowd of attendees, including elected leaders and city and county managers from across the region. More than 770 individuals have since watched the broadcast on YouTube. The full forum can be viewed at: https://www.youtube.com/live/MW0TxL89yQM?si=t9i-0zFcxKyKxlKh

McDonald: 'Your voices are being heard'

Alamogordo Mayor Sharon McDonald said the public response to the Bonito Lake issue has reached well beyond the city limits.

“The public response regarding Bonito Lake has been remarkable. I have received emails, calls, and text messages from people across New Mexico and as far away as Texas,” McDonald said. “Although I have not responded to everyone individually, I have read every email and reviewed every message. I want to respond collectively and assure you that your voices are being heard.”

“This is what meaningful citizen engagement looks like. Elected officials can serve most effectively when citizens speak up, share their concerns, and remain involved. I am proud of the respectful and passionate outreach from people who care deeply about Bonito Lake and its future.”

McDonald added that she “is encouraged by support from county officials and state legislators for keeping the lake open.”

“I will continue listening and working toward a responsible path that protects our water supply while preserving Bonito Lake’s important role in fishing, recreation, and family traditions,” she said. “Thank you to everyone who has reached out. Your involvement matters, and it is making a difference.”

A reversal, but not a retreat

Reading from prepared remarks — something he acknowledged he rarely does — Stockwell traced his history with the lake back to 1992, when he first managed the city and concluded that the lake’s role as the single best water source in the city’s inventory had to come before recreation. He noted the lake was already about 40 percent silted in during the 1990s, a problem that went unaddressed until the devastating 2023 fires and debris flows forced its closure. After restoration, water began flowing consistently to the city again in 2026.

Stockwell was at times defiant in defending his original recommendation to close the lake entirely, stressing that the detention basins, ponds, and drainage systems built to intercept debris have left surrounding areas hazardous. Former parking areas, he said, are now subject to mud flows that would have trapped vehicles during this summer’s storms. His comments returned again and again to a single theme: the lake was purchased in the 1950s as a water source, and protecting the city’s drinking water comes first.

But citing constructive public input and interest from state officials — including Sen. Townsend and the legislative representatives of the region, who have agreed to convene legislative colleagues and state agencies — Stockwell outlined five recommendations he will bring to the commission on Sept. 22:

1. Direct the city manager to open discussions with the state, Otero County, Lincoln County, and Ruidoso officials on options that preserve Alamogordo’s water supply while exploring compatible recreation at the lake and surrounding areas.

2. Continue construction of the remaining debris-flow protection projects.

3. Construct required security fencing around the dam structure and ancillary facilities only — not the lake itself.

4. Maintain the status quo allowing public access for fishing.

5. Post additional signage advising visitors that the lake is a primary municipal water source and that anyone entering city property does so at their own risk.

Stockwell also proposed a six-month deadline to report back to the commission on the results of the regional discussions.

A campaign promise in action

McDonald ran on a platform of supporting more transparency and getting people more involved in the conversation on a regional basis — one block at a time. A nongovernmental sponsored forum convening mayors from multiple cities in the region, alongside a dialogue with community members from across the area, reflects exactly that commitment to healthy debate and open governance — the kind of civic engagement that is the cornerstone of a vibrant and active local government in the region. Stay tuned for more updates and the public is still encouraged to attend the upcoming commission meeting and the one on Sept 22, 2026 to make public comment and keep the pressure ongoing.

item.title: In Memory of Evelyn Bernice Nowell Webb
item.description:
Evelyn Bernice Nowell Webb went home to her lord on August 27, 2026, at the age of 83.

Evelyn was born to Leon and Mary Nowell on November 17, 1942, in Alamogordo , New Mexico. She grew up in Tularosa and graduated from Tularosa High School in 1960. Later that same year, she married the love of her life, Dennis Webb.

Evelyn's love of adventure and travel began during her early years with Dennis.While he served in the Marine Corps, they lived in California, Arizona and North Carolina. Later in life Evelyn was blessed with the opportunity to see even more of the world. She visited 28 different countries an loved nothing more than sharing the stories and memories of her adventures with others.

Throughout her life, Evelyn wore many hats. She cleaned rooms, waited tables, worked as a telephone operator, and eventually retired from the State pf New Mrexico as an executive secretary. Whatever she was doing, she brought her own warmth, humor and personality to it.

Evelyn was a longtime member of the Tularosa Church of the Nazarene. When the Tularosa church closed, she became a member of Angus Church of the Nazarene. Her Faith was an important part of her life, and she faithfully served her church as a member of the church board, church secretary and treasurer.

Those who knew Evelyn will remember her wonderful sense of humor, her love of a good joke and a good giggle, and, most of all, her beautiful smile. She had a way of bringing joy and laugher to those around her. Her wit, humor and loving spirit will be deeply missed by all who had the privilege of knowing her.

Evelyn was preceded in death by her parents; three sisters; her brother; her husband, Dennis Webb; son, Dennis Webb Jr; and her daughter, Cheryl Parker.

She leaved behind to cherish her memory her son, Brandon Webb of Colorado Springs, CO; daughter, Beverly Brazel (Joe) of Capitan, NM; grandchildren, Keena Brazel of Capitan, New Mexico; Micharl Brazel (Janet) of Tucumcari, New Mexico; Cameron Parker of Tularosa, New Mexico; Dennis Webb (Samantha) of Spanaway, Washington; her beloved great-granddaughters, Avery, Adalynn and Willow Eve, who were the light and joy of her life; and her sister, Joyce Yearlt of Fort Collins, Colorado.

In lieu of flowers, Evelyn requested that donations be made to Bonita Park Campground.

A celebration of Evelyn's life will be held September 5, 2026, at 11:00 a.m. at Angus Church of the Nazarene, located at 103 Bonita Park, Angus, New Mexico. Lunch will follow at the same location.
